capstone.title: Sensor acquisition system
capstone.subtitle: Build a sensor acquisition chain or calibrate a temperature monitor.
capstone.description: Four milestones build one shared project. Repair three deliberate faults, then qualify the complete system with real ngspice and Icarus.

lessons.title: 01 · Your first measured circuit
lessons.summary: Inspect a source, resistor and capacitor; predict the time constant and verify a transient.

steps.title: Predict the response
steps.instructions: For R = 10 kΩ and C = 1 nF, what is the time constant?
steps.explanation: The product R·C is 10 µs. One time constant reaches about 63% of a step.

steps.title: Find the three devices
steps.instructions: Choose Open workspace. Select V1, R1 and C1 in the Design tree; their values and nets appear in the inspector. Ground is net 0. Return to this guide through View → Student lesson guide.

steps.title: Measure one time constant
steps.instructions: Choose Run lesson, then Results. Probe vout at 12 µs: the input stepped to 1.8 V at 2 µs. Expect 1.08–1.20 V. Check this step after the run finishes.

steps.title: Explain your result
steps.instructions: Why does the capacitor voltage rise gradually? Record the measured voltage and the time relative to the input edge. Record at least 40 characters. This is a written reflection, not an automatically graded engineering claim.

lessons.title: 02 · Nets, ground and loading
lessons.summary: Complete a divider by placing and connecting the lower resistor, then verify its output.

steps.title: Predict a divider
steps.instructions: Two equal 10 kΩ resistors divide a 1.8 V supply. What is the unloaded output?
steps.explanation: Equal resistors split the voltage equally when the output is unloaded.

steps.title: Place and wire the lower resistor
steps.instructions: Open workspace. The starter has V1 and R1 but no lower resistor. Choose Component → Resistor, place it below R1, and select it. Set its name to R2, Value to 10k, p terminal to out and n terminal to 0 in Properties. Apply the edit. R1 already connects vin to out. Check the named nets even if the symbols are far apart.

steps.title: Verify the operating point
steps.instructions: Run lesson. Inspect out in Results and confirm 0.9 V within 1 mV.

steps.title: Explain your result
steps.instructions: Describe the path from V1 through R1 and R2 to ground. Explain why a disconnected terminal is different from an unconnected-looking drawing. Record at least 40 characters. This is a written reflection, not an automatically graded engineering claim.

lessons.title: 03 · Change, compare and undo
lessons.summary: Make a deliberate parameter change and prove its effect using a new result.

steps.title: Predict a design change
steps.instructions: Doubling R while keeping C fixed changes the time constant how?
steps.explanation: The time constant is proportional to R.

steps.title: Double the resistor
steps.instructions: Select R1 in the schematic and change its Value from 10k to 20k. Apply the property edit. Try Undo and Redo, ending at 20k.

steps.title: Measure the slower response
steps.instructions: Run the edited design. At 22 µs, vout should be 1.08–1.20 V: one 20 µs time constant after the edge. An earlier run will not pass this check.

steps.title: Explain your result
steps.instructions: Compare the original and edited waveforms. Explain why reusing a result captured before the resistor edit would be misleading. Record at least 40 characters. This is a written reflection, not an automatically graded engineering claim.

lessons.title: 04 · Reusable cells and hierarchy
lessons.summary: Inspect a two-resistor cell instantiated in a testbench.

steps.title: Distinguish master and instance
steps.instructions: If two instances refer to the same cell, editing the cell changes which implementation?
steps.explanation: Instances refer to the shared cell implementation; instance parameters can differ where supported.

steps.title: Follow the instance ports
steps.instructions: Open the divider cell from the Design tree. It has IN, OUT and GND ports. Return to top and inspect XDIV mappings to vin, out and 0.

steps.title: Simulate through hierarchy
steps.instructions: Run lesson using the top-level testbench. Confirm out is still 0.9 V.

steps.title: Explain your result
steps.instructions: Explain what belongs in the reusable divider cell and what belongs in its testbench. Name the three port mappings. Record at least 40 characters. This is a written reflection, not an automatically graded engineering claim.

lessons.title: 05 · Requirements and debugging
lessons.summary: Distinguish a successful simulator run from meeting a design requirement.

steps.title: Reason about loading
steps.instructions: Adding a 10 kΩ load across the lower 10 kΩ divider resistor makes the output…
steps.explanation: The parallel resistance decreases. The loaded output is 0.6 V.

steps.title: Reduce loading
steps.instructions: The goal is to keep out above 0.89 V. Select Rload and increase its Value to 1Meg. Keep the divider resistors at 10k.

steps.title: Check the requirement
steps.instructions: Run lesson and verify out is between 0.89 and 0.91 V. A completed simulation can still miss a requirement.

steps.title: Explain your result
steps.instructions: Record the achieved voltage. Explain the load-resistance tradeoff and one condition the simple DC test does not cover. Record at least 40 characters. This is a written reflection, not an automatically graded engineering claim.

lessons.title: 06 · Layout, checks and reproducibility
lessons.summary: Inspect geometry, understand evidence limits, and preserve a reproducible learning record.

steps.title: Interpret physical checks
steps.instructions: What does passing generic teaching DRC establish?
options: Only the implemented generic rules were satisfied
steps.explanation: A foundry-qualified rule deck, extraction and other signoff evidence are separate.

steps.title: Inspect the matched geometry
steps.instructions: Open workspace and switch to Layout. Fit the view and inspect the common-centroid arrangement. Use Analysis → Geometry DRC to read the actual findings. This checkpoint only verifies geometry is present.

steps.title: Save the exact project
steps.instructions: Use Save work in the guide, then check this step. Close/reopen the lesson from the Hub to resume the saved project.

steps.title: Explain your result
steps.instructions: Record one geometry finding or limitation, the project location, and what you would include in a reproducible handoff beyond a screenshot. Record at least 40 characters. This is a written reflection, not an automatically graded engineering claim.

lessons.title: 01 · Design around source and load
lessons.summary: Model loading explicitly before adding gain.

steps.title: Calculate the loaded divider
steps.instructions: R1 = R2 = Rload = 10 kΩ with 1.8 V input. What is out?

steps.title: Add the output load
steps.instructions: Open workspace. Add a generic resistor with Component → Resistor. Name it Rload, set Value to 10k, and assign p to out and n to 0 in Properties. Apply. It is now in parallel with R2. Keep R1 and R2 at 10k.

steps.title: Verify the loaded value
steps.instructions: Run lesson and measure out. The expected interval is 0.599–0.601 V.

steps.title: Explain your result
steps.instructions: Explain why a measurement instrument or following stage can change the voltage. Propose a way to reduce this effect. Record at least 40 characters. This is a written reflection, not an automatically graded engineering claim.

lessons.title: 02 · Set bandwidth with an RC pole
lessons.summary: Choose capacitance for a target bandwidth and verify the AC response.

steps.title: Predict the pole
steps.instructions: R = 10 kΩ, C = 2 nF. Approximately where is the −3 dB pole?
steps.explanation: The pole is 1/(2πRC), approximately 7.96 kHz.

steps.title: Set the capacitance
steps.instructions: Change C1 Value from 1n to 2n. The AC source amplitude is 1 V, so output magnitude directly represents gain.

steps.title: Measure the pole
steps.instructions: Run lesson. Inspect vout near 8 kHz; expect magnitude 0.68–0.73 V, approximately −3 dB.

steps.title: Explain your result
steps.instructions: Record the measured magnitude and explain why increasing capacitance reduces bandwidth. Record at least 40 characters. This is a written reflection, not an automatically graded engineering claim.

lessons.title: 03 · Scale a current mirror
lessons.summary: Use geometry ratios to set bias current and inspect the operating point.

steps.title: Predict mirror scaling
steps.instructions: For equal lengths and similar VDS, doubling only MOUT width approximately…
steps.explanation: In the educational model, matched overdrive and doubled W/L approximately double current.

steps.title: Set a 2:1 mirror
steps.instructions: Open current_mirror, select MOUT, and set width w to 4u; MREF remains 2u with the same length. The reference current is 10 µA.

steps.title: Check output current
steps.instructions: Run lesson and inspect current through VOUT. Its magnitude should be 18–23 µA; the source supplies current into the mirror.

steps.title: Explain your result
steps.instructions: Record the output current and explain why unequal drain voltages and insufficient output headroom can spoil the ideal ratio. Record at least 40 characters. This is a written reflection, not an automatically graded engineering claim.

lessons.title: 04 · Steer a differential pair
lessons.summary: Apply a small differential input and follow the change in branch voltages.

steps.title: Predict the balanced state
steps.instructions: With equal inputs and matched devices, how does the tail current divide?
steps.explanation: Symmetry gives equal branch currents while both devices remain in the intended region.

steps.title: Apply a differential input
steps.instructions: In differential_pair_testbench, change VIN Value to 5m. It is connected between inp and inn, so the common-mode source remains separate.

steps.title: Observe current steering
steps.instructions: Run lesson. outp should move below outn. Check the difference outn − outp is positive and below 0.1 V.

steps.title: Explain your result
steps.instructions: Explain which transistor takes more current and why its drain voltage falls through the load resistor. State the common-mode limitation. Record at least 40 characters. This is a written reflection, not an automatically graded engineering claim.

lessons.title: 05 · A five-transistor amplifier
lessons.summary: Combine bias, differential input and active load, then measure small-signal gain.

steps.title: Choose the correct analysis
steps.instructions: Which analysis measures small-signal gain around a solved operating point?
steps.explanation: AC linearizes the devices around their bias point.

steps.title: Inspect the five devices
steps.instructions: Open amplifier. Follow M1/M2, the M3/M4 active load, and the M5 bias device. Return to amplifier_testbench before measuring.

steps.title: Measure low-frequency gain
steps.instructions: Run lesson with the supplied AC setup and inspect out at 10 Hz. The teaching-model target is magnitude above 5 V/V and below 10000 V/V.

steps.title: Explain your result
steps.instructions: Record gain, identify the bias and load assumptions, and describe the next checks: output swing, stability in feedback, noise, PVT and extracted parasitics. Record at least 40 characters. This is a written reflection, not an automatically graded engineering claim.

lessons.title: 06 · Matching and physical tradeoffs
lessons.summary: Inspect common-centroid geometry and plan a credible analog implementation.

steps.title: Identify what centroid placement helps
steps.instructions: Common-centroid placement primarily helps cancel…
steps.explanation: Symmetric placement can cancel some first-order gradients; random mismatch and routing remain.

steps.title: Inspect symmetry and routing
steps.instructions: Open Layout. Compare the repeated resistor units and their placement about the center. Inspect layers and dimensions; this structural check does not certify matching.

steps.title: Preserve the reviewed geometry
steps.instructions: Use Save work, then check. Explore the existing extraction and physical-verification tools through the feature map; do not call generic geometry a foundry-qualified layout.

steps.title: Explain your result
steps.instructions: Write a short layout review: symmetry, routing resistance, dummy devices, required process deck, and the schematic-versus-extracted comparisons you would run. Record at least 40 characters. This is a written reflection, not an automatically graded engineering claim.

lessons.title: 07 · Understand gm/ID and choose a bias
lessons.summary: Measure transconductance efficiency and connect gate bias to current, gain and headroom.

steps.title: Reason before editing
steps.instructions: A transistor has gm = 200 µS and ID = 20 µA. What is gm/ID?
steps.explanation: 200 µS / 20 µA = 10 V⁻¹. gm is the small-signal slope of drain current versus gate voltage at the bias point.

steps.title: Build or repair the design
steps.instructions: Open workspace. Select VG, change Value from .85 to .65, and Apply changes. Keep M1 at W=10u and L=1u, with VD=1 V. Predict gm/ID using VOV=.65−.45=.20 V.

steps.title: Verify the requirement
steps.instructions: Run lesson, then check this step. The operating point must give gm/ID between 9.8 and 10.2 V⁻¹, ID between 20 and 21 µA, and at least .70 V headroom. The checkpoint captures the measured values.

steps.title: Write your design review
steps.instructions: Report ID, gm and gm/ID with units. Explain why lowering overdrive improves current efficiency in this teaching model, and why this model cannot establish weak-inversion performance. Record at least 40 characters. This writing is saved for review, not automatically graded for correctness.

lessons.title: 08 · Turn a gm target into device width
lessons.summary: Work from a transconductance requirement to bias current and width, then verify the operating point.

steps.title: Reason before editing
steps.instructions: For gm=200 µS and gm/ID=10 V⁻¹, what drain current is required?
steps.explanation: ID = gm / (gm/ID) = 200 µS / 10 V⁻¹ = 20 µA.

steps.title: Build or repair the design
steps.instructions: Read Learn first. Keep VG=.65, VD=1 and L=1u. Select M1 and set Width to 9.804u, then Apply changes. Use the width estimate to meet gm=200 µS at ID=20 µA.

steps.title: Verify the requirement
steps.instructions: Run lesson. Check ID=19.8–20.2 µA, gm=198–202 µS and gm/ID=9.8–10.2 V⁻¹. A width entry alone does not prove the bias meets the requirement.

steps.title: Write your design review
steps.instructions: Write the chain specification → gm → ID → ID/W → W. State which bias conditions must match the lookup point, and which checks would still be needed for an amplifier. Record at least 40 characters. This writing is saved for review, not automatically graded for correctness.

lessons.title: 09 · Budget voltage headroom
lessons.summary: Repair a bias point that loses saturation and explain output swing constraints.

steps.title: Reason before editing
steps.instructions: In the teaching model, VGS=.65 V and VTH=.45 V. With VDS=.10 V, is M1 in saturation?
options: No: VDS is below VOV=.20 V
steps.explanation: Turning a device on does not guarantee saturation. This model requires VDS ≥ VOV; extra margin supports signal swing.

steps.title: Build or repair the design
steps.instructions: Select VD and change Value from .1 to .4. Keep VG=.65, W=10u and L=1u. Apply changes. Predict the headroom VDS−VOV.

steps.title: Verify the requirement
steps.instructions: Run lesson. Verify .19–.21 V headroom, gm/ID=9.8–10.2 V⁻¹ and ID=19.8–20.5 µA. Compare against a run of the original low-drain-voltage case.

steps.title: Write your design review
steps.instructions: Explain why the initial device is on but outside saturation. Sketch a voltage budget for two stacked devices and describe how signal swing consumes margin. Record at least 40 characters. This writing is saved for review, not automatically graded for correctness.

lessons.title: 10 · Trade transistor area for current at fixed gm
lessons.summary: Meet the same gm target at lower current and identify what the simple model cannot tell you.

steps.title: Reason before editing
steps.instructions: Holding gm=200 µS, changing gm/ID from 10 to 20 V⁻¹ changes ID from…
steps.explanation: For fixed gm, doubling gm/ID halves current. Area, capacitance, speed and noise still need separate evaluation.

steps.title: Build or repair the design
steps.instructions: Select VG and set Value=.55; set M1 Width=19.608u, keeping L=1u and VD=1. Apply changes. The lower overdrive needs more width to preserve gm.

steps.title: Verify the requirement
steps.instructions: Run lesson. Require gm=198–202 µS, ID=9.8–10.2 µA, and gm/ID=19.6–20.4 V⁻¹. Compare this bias with the 9.804 µm width design.

steps.title: Write your design review
steps.instructions: Compare current, width and gm between both designs. Explain why this experiment cannot prove speed or noise superiority. Specify a real-PDK characterization and verification plan. Record at least 40 characters. This writing is saved for review, not automatically graded for correctness.

lessons.title: 01 · Truth tables and combinational RTL
lessons.summary: Enumerate the complete truth table for XOR and a two-input mux.

steps.title: Predict the behavior
steps.instructions: When a=b=1, XOR is…
steps.explanation: XOR is one only when its inputs differ.

steps.title: Inspect the design and reference bench
steps.instructions: Read assign parity and assign mux. Open lab_tb.sv to see all eight input combinations; edit the RTL, not the reference testbench.

steps.title: Run the reference checks
steps.instructions: Choose Run lesson. Open Results to inspect the digital workspace. Check this step only after simulation completes. A modified reference testbench cannot earn this checkpoint.

steps.title: Explain your result
steps.instructions: Explain the difference between XOR and OR, and how the mux select chooses its output. Record at least 40 characters. This is a written reflection, not an automatically graded engineering claim.

lessons.title: 02 · Clock, reset and enable
lessons.summary: Verify reset, hold, increment and four-bit wraparound.

steps.title: Predict the behavior
steps.instructions: A four-bit unsigned counter increments from 15 to…
steps.explanation: Four bits retain values 0 through 15; the carry is discarded.

steps.title: Inspect the design and reference bench
steps.instructions: Read the positive-edge always block. Follow reset priority and the enable condition. The testbench covers enabled and held cycles plus wraparound.

steps.title: Run the reference checks
steps.instructions: Choose Run lesson. Open Results to inspect the digital workspace. Check this step only after simulation completes. A modified reference testbench cannot earn this checkpoint.

steps.title: Explain your result
steps.instructions: Explain why nonblocking assignments are used for state and what happens while enable is low. Record at least 40 characters. This is a written reflection, not an automatically graded engineering claim.

lessons.title: 03 · State and one-cycle handshakes
lessons.summary: Turn a held request into a single clock-wide pulse.

steps.title: Predict the behavior
steps.instructions: A rising-edge detector needs…
steps.explanation: Comparing current and previous request distinguishes a new edge from a held level.

steps.title: Inspect the design and reference bench
steps.instructions: Follow previous and pulse in the RTL. The testbench holds requests for several clocks; every rising request must produce exactly one pulse.

steps.title: Run the reference checks
steps.instructions: Choose Run lesson. Open Results to inspect the digital workspace. Check this step only after simulation completes. A modified reference testbench cannot earn this checkpoint.

steps.title: Explain your result
steps.instructions: Explain why a level-sensitive request cannot be treated as a new transaction on every clock. Record at least 40 characters. This is a written reflection, not an automatically graded engineering claim.

lessons.title: 04 · Counters as waveform generators
lessons.summary: Sweep duty settings and count actual high cycles in each eight-clock frame.

steps.title: Predict the behavior
steps.instructions: A duty setting of 3 over an eight-clock frame gives…
steps.explanation: The comparator is high for phases 0, 1 and 2.

steps.title: Inspect the design and reference bench
steps.instructions: Inspect phase and the phase < duty comparator. The reference bench checks every duty setting, including zero. This is synchronous PWM, not a modeled analog power stage.

steps.title: Run the reference checks
steps.instructions: Choose Run lesson. Open Results to inspect the digital workspace. Check this step only after simulation completes. A modified reference testbench cannot earn this checkpoint.

steps.title: Explain your result
steps.instructions: Record one duty ratio and explain the resolution/frequency tradeoff when the counter width changes. Record at least 40 characters. This is a written reflection, not an automatically graded engineering claim.

lessons.title: 05 · Fixed-point arithmetic and valid data
lessons.summary: Accumulate four samples without overflow and round the result.

steps.title: Predict the behavior
steps.instructions: Four unsigned four-bit samples require a sum width of…
steps.explanation: The maximum sum is 60, which needs six unsigned bits.

steps.title: Inspect the design and reference bench
steps.instructions: Trace sum, total and count. The reference bench inserts invalid cycles and maximum inputs, checking rounding and ready pulses.

steps.title: Run the reference checks
steps.instructions: Choose Run lesson. Open Results to inspect the digital workspace. Check this step only after simulation completes. A modified reference testbench cannot earn this checkpoint.

steps.title: Explain your result
steps.instructions: Explain why the current sample must be included before division and how invalid cycles affect the counter. Record at least 40 characters. This is a written reflection, not an automatically graded engineering claim.

lessons.title: 06 · A verified serial transmitter
lessons.summary: Frame bytes with start/stop bits, capture the payload and handle reset.

steps.title: Predict the behavior
steps.instructions: After accepting a byte, changing the input data should…
steps.explanation: The accepted payload is captured in a shift register until the frame completes.

steps.title: Inspect the design and reference bench
steps.instructions: Read frame and bit_index. Each lab clock is one bit period. The bench checks 00, FF, A5 and 3C plus mid-frame reset. Use the Digital workspace for waveforms and optional synthesis; baud generation and reception are later extensions.

steps.title: Run the reference checks
steps.instructions: Choose Run lesson. Open Results to inspect the digital workspace. Check this step only after simulation completes. A modified reference testbench cannot earn this checkpoint.

steps.title: Explain your result
steps.instructions: Describe the interface contract, reset behavior, and what additional checks would be needed for a real UART with independent clocks. Record at least 40 characters. This is a written reflection, not an automatically graded engineering claim.

lessons.title: 07 · Repair unintended combinational memory
lessons.summary: Fix an incomplete combinational assignment and prove the output depends only on current inputs.

steps.title: Reason before editing
steps.instructions: What hardware can an unassigned output branch in combinational RTL infer?
steps.explanation: If an output must retain its old value on a branch, the design implies storage.

steps.title: Build or repair the design
steps.instructions: Open RTL. In mux_repair.sv, assign y for BOTH select values inside always @*. When select=0, y must be a; when select=1, y must be b. Keep the reference testbench unchanged.

steps.title: Verify the requirement
steps.instructions: Run lesson before editing to observe the failure. After repair, Run lesson again and inspect Results. The independent reference bench must complete every assertion. Compilation alone, a stale run, or an edited reference bench does not pass.

steps.title: Write your design review
steps.instructions: Explain the missing assignment, a concrete sequence that exposes stale output, and why a truth table must be checked after different input histories. Record at least 40 characters. This writing is saved for review, not automatically graded for correctness.

lessons.title: 08 · Repair arithmetic overflow
lessons.summary: Define an arithmetic contract and repair a four-bit saturating accumulator.

steps.title: Reason before editing
steps.instructions: A four-bit unsigned saturating accumulator holds 13 and accepts 5. What is the next value?
steps.explanation: The mathematical sum is 18, above the maximum 15. Saturation clips to 15; wrapping would produce 2.

steps.title: Build or repair the design
steps.instructions: Open RTL. Keep the five-bit total so the carry is visible. Replace the wrapping update with a comparison: if total > 15, assign 15; otherwise assign total[3:0]. Preserve synchronous reset priority and hold sum when valid=0.

steps.title: Verify the requirement
steps.instructions: Run lesson before editing to observe the failure. After repair, Run lesson again and inspect Results. The independent reference bench must complete every assertion. Compilation alone, a stale run, or an edited reference bench does not pass.

steps.title: Write your design review
steps.instructions: Show 13+5 under mathematical, wrapping and saturating arithmetic. Explain intermediate width, reset priority, invalid-cycle hold and one boundary test. Record at least 40 characters. This writing is saved for review, not automatically graded for correctness.

lessons.title: 09 · Align data and valid through a pipeline
lessons.summary: Repair a one-cycle validity mismatch and reason about bubbles, reset and timing.

steps.title: Reason before editing
steps.instructions: Stage captures an input at edge k and result captures stage at edge k+1. Which validity belongs with result after k+1?
steps.explanation: Nonblocking assignments read the previous register values. Data and validity need identical register latency.

steps.title: Build or repair the design
steps.instructions: Open RTL. The data has two registers: stage and result. Repair valid_out to use stage_valid rather than valid_in. Keep nonblocking assignments and reset clearing both valid registers. This interface accepts one item per clock and has no backpressure.

steps.title: Verify the requirement
steps.instructions: Run lesson before editing to observe the failure. After repair, Run lesson again and inspect Results. The independent reference bench must complete every assertion. Compilation alone, a stale run, or an edited reference bench does not pass.

steps.title: Write your design review
steps.instructions: Draw an edge-by-edge data/valid table including a bubble and mid-stream reset. Explain latency versus throughput and why passing RTL simulation is not a timing-closure result. Record at least 40 characters. This writing is saved for review, not automatically graded for correctness.

lessons.title: 01 · Cross the analog/digital boundary
lessons.summary: Follow the clocked bridge from comparator voltage to RTL decisions and back to DAC voltages.

steps.title: Calculate one code step
steps.instructions: A four-bit converter spans 1.8 V. One LSB is…
steps.explanation: 1.8/16 = 0.1125 V per code step.

steps.title: Inspect both cells
steps.instructions: Open workspace for the native circuit, then RTL for sar_controller. Locate the DAC, held node and comparator. Read the bridge tab in Mixed-signal experiment.

steps.title: Follow the four decisions
steps.instructions: Run lesson. For 0.93 V expect code 8 at edge 7. Results opens the edge table and analog waveforms.

steps.title: Explain your result
steps.instructions: Follow one loop: DAC code → voltage → comparator → sampled bit → next trial. Explain the purpose of the ambiguous-voltage region. Record at least 40 characters. This is a written reflection, not an automatically graded engineering claim.

lessons.title: 02 · Acquire, then hold
lessons.summary: Change the input during conversion and verify the held sample is used.

steps.title: Predict a held conversion
steps.instructions: The input changes after the sampling switch opens. Ideally, the conversion represents…
steps.explanation: The capacitor retains the acquired voltage while the SAR searches.

steps.title: Inspect the hold capacitor
steps.instructions: Select Chold and verify 20p. In bridge configuration, vin steps from 0.93 to 0.2 V after 3.5 µs.

steps.title: Verify retained analog state
steps.instructions: Run lesson. Despite the later input change, code 8 must complete at edge 7.

steps.title: Explain your result
steps.instructions: Compare vin and held during conversion. Identify charge leakage and switch charge injection as real effects absent or simplified in this teaching model. Record at least 40 characters. This is a written reflection, not an automatically graded engineering claim.

lessons.title: 03 · Quantization and code transitions
lessons.summary: Predict a new output code and verify an edited stimulus.

steps.title: Predict the code
steps.instructions: For 1.2 V with a 1.8 V reference, floor(16·Vin/Vref) is…
steps.explanation: The scaled value is approximately 10.67, giving code 10.

steps.title: Set a new input
steps.instructions: Open Mixed-signal experiment, set Input voltage to 1.2, and Apply configuration. Return to the guide.

steps.title: Verify the new code
steps.instructions: Run lesson. Expect code 10 at edge 7. Inspect the different trial sequence.

steps.title: Explain your result
steps.instructions: State the input interval represented by code 10. Explain why an exact boundary can be sensitive to comparator offset and settling. Record at least 40 characters. This is a written reflection, not an automatically graded engineering claim.

lessons.title: 04 · Repair a timing failure
lessons.summary: A deliberately fast clock produces a wrong conversion; restore enough settling time.

steps.title: Relate clock and analog settling
steps.instructions: Shortening the clock without changing the DAC can…
options: Sample the DAC before it settles
steps.explanation: Analog networks need time to approach the trial voltage.

steps.title: Restore the comparison period
steps.instructions: First run the fast 10 ns setup and inspect the wrong code. Then open Mixed-signal experiment and change Clock period to 1u; Apply configuration. The smaller analog step can remain.

steps.title: Recover the correct conversion
steps.instructions: Run the repaired design. The 0.3 V input must produce code 2 at edge 7.

steps.title: Explain your result
steps.instructions: Record the failing and repaired codes and explain the settling-time versus conversion-rate tradeoff. Record at least 40 characters. This is a written reflection, not an automatically graded engineering claim.

lessons.title: 05 · Repair a DAC weight
lessons.summary: Use a numerical requirement to locate and repair a wrong resistor.

steps.title: Understand the MSB weight
steps.instructions: Which DAC resistor has the largest conductance?
steps.explanation: The MSB branch has the smallest resistance and greatest weight.

steps.title: Repair the MSB branch
steps.instructions: Run the supplied faulty circuit once. Inspect Rbit3: its 20k value is wrong. Change it to 10k and apply the property edit.

steps.title: Check against the unchanged reference
steps.instructions: Run the repaired design. The expected code remains 8 at edge 7 for 0.93 V.

steps.title: Explain your result
steps.instructions: Explain why changing the expected code to match the faulty circuit would hide the design problem. Record the before/after codes. Record at least 40 characters. This is a written reflection, not an automatically graded engineering claim.

steps.title: Size the input pair with gm/ID

Open workspace to view the Miller core. M1 and M2 share the tail current; M5 mirrors the current set by M8. CC1 and CC2 connect the high-impedance first-stage node to OUT. Identify the two gain stages and the source/body ties.

For a first estimate use gm ≈ 2π·fu·Cc, with Cc the sum of CC1 and CC2. For 1 MHz and 4 pF this is about 25 µS. Pick a measured gm/ID region. Choose Run testbenches, then Results → Device bias. Record M2 gm, ID, gm/ID and saturation margin. lessons.title: Why layout choices matter
lessons.summary: Fix via enclosure and matching, find a geometry-clean open, then improve the actual bandwidth of an RC route.

steps.title: Start from physical intent
steps.instructions: A layout has clean width and spacing checks. Which additional check answers whether the extracted circuit has the intended devices and connectivity?
steps.explanation: DRC checks geometry against rules. LVS compares extracted devices and connectivity with the reference schematic. Use both before trusting extraction.

steps.title: Enclose a via in both layers
steps.instructions:
Choose Open workspace for the via cross-layer coupon. Each 0.50 × 0.50 µm metal pad surrounds a 0.15 µm cut. Its right edge initially extends past the pad by 0.05 µm. In Properties → Geometry (µm), set the via’s left edge to 0.175 µm and keep its y at 0.175 µm.

Check the overlap on metal1 and metal2. Imagine overlay error shifting the cut toward a metal edge. Explain why a borderline or missing enclosure can make a resistive or open contact. Larger arrays can reduce via resistance and current per cut, subject to spacing and current rules.

steps.title: Reject a linear process gradient
steps.instructions:
Open workspace for the four equal unit tiles. The initial AABB centers are 0.2, 1.0, 1.8 and 2.6 µm. Calculate the mean position of each pair. Move a tile from each group to produce ABBA (or BAAB) with the same four slots. Keep 0.40 µm units and at least 0.20 µm separation.

Place equal devices together when matching matters. Keep the same orientation and local surroundings. In a real array use appropriate edge dummies, symmetric contacts and routes, and equal current density. A common centroid cancels a first-order spatial gradient of equal units. Random mismatch and gradients with curvature still matter.

steps.title: Find an open that can pass geometry checks
steps.instructions:
Open workspace for the RC routing cell. Identify the resistor-to-capacitor metal1 path, its two endpoints, and the separate ground plate. Select just the vout path, delete it, and compare Geometry DRC with the linked connectivity check. The pads can obey spacing while the physical signal path is open.

Undo the deletion. Check this step after restoring continuity. Linked checks compare labelled terminal connectivity in this teaching fixture. For a real circuit, use the technology’s extracted netlist and LVS deck, then inspect shorts, opens, body ties, and pin order.

steps.title: Measure the bandwidth penalty
steps.instructions:
The schematic has 1 kΩ and 10 fF. Calculate f₃dB ≈ 1/(2πRC). The layout uses an approximately 22.67 µm path with 0.20 µm width and a teaching coefficient of 2 Ω/□. Predict R ≈ R□·L/W.

Choose Compare route RC, then Results. Inspect the before and after bandwidth and the modeled 12.5 GHz requirement. Open Before / after waveforms to see the two AC responses. The same schematic, sweep, and target apply to both. The thin route should miss the target.

steps.title: Meet the target without wasting metal
steps.instructions:
Select just the vout path in Layout. Try widths of 0.40 µm and 0.80 µm and run Compare route RC after each edit. Keep the path endpoints and the schematic the same. Choose a width that gives at least 12.5 GHz.

Wider metal lowers resistance and current density, but increases area capacitance. Shortening a route lowers both. A parallel aggressor can add coupling, especially across a small gap or long overlap. In a sensitive high-impedance or clocked circuit, consider spacing, a quiet shield with a proper return, or fewer parallel runs. A shield also adds capacitance.

steps.title: Record your design reasoning
steps.instructions: Record the three widths and their extracted resistance, capacitance and bandwidth. Explain why wider metal did not automatically help. Describe one matching or coupling decision and the DRC, LVS, extracted simulation, or reliability check you would use for an actual process.

lessons.title: LC filters and Bode plots
lessons.summary: Hand-sketch, simulate and tune low-pass, high-pass, band-pass and notch responses on one editable RLC bench.

steps.title: Read the axes
steps.instructions: A Bode plot uses logarithmic frequency, voltage gain in dB, and a separate phase axis. A low-pass gain changes from −20 dB at 10 kHz to −60 dB at 100 kHz. What is the slope?
steps.explanation: 100 kHz / 10 kHz = 10, so the frequency increased one decade and the magnitude fell 40 dB.

steps.title: Count poles and zeros
steps.instructions: A low-pass second-order denominator has two poles and a constant numerator. Far above its break, what happens to gain?
options: It falls at about 40 dB per decade
It stays flat because the poles cancel
It rises at 40 dB per decade
steps.explanation: Each pole subtracts 20 dB/decade in the high-frequency asymptote. Each zero adds 20. At the origin the factor contributes its slope from the first plotted frequency.

steps.title: Sketch and measure four filters
steps.instructions:
Open workspace and follow the four series RLC branches. The output is across C for low-pass, L for high-pass, R for band-pass, and the series LC pair for notch. VIN is 1 V AC. Use H = Vout/Vin, magnitude 20 log₁₀|H| and phase arg(H).

Calculate f₀ = 1/(2π√LC) and Q = √(L/C)/R. Draw a logarithmic axis with five equal-spaced points at 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10 and 100 times f₀. Mark the asymptotes. LP is flat then −40 dB/decade, HP is +40 then flat, BP is +20 then −20. The notch approaches 0 dB at both ends and has a zero at f₀.

Run AC sweep and open Results. Select each output and toggle the dashed hand-sketch guide. Read the phase and exact measured dB at f₀. At a true notch null phase is undefined. The graph floors magnitude at −100 dB to keep the rolloff visible.

steps.title: Change Q without moving f₀
steps.instructions:
Record the original low-pass peak and phase. Change only RLP from 220 Ω to about 470 Ω. With 10 mH and 100 nF, Q falls from 1.44 to about 0.67. Compare the new AC run to your prediction. A lower Q damps the peak while leaving the natural frequency unchanged.

Mark −90° at f₀ and measure the magnitude there. Only a second-order low-pass with Q = 1/√2 gives −3 dB at f₀ relative to the DC gain. Distinguish that special case from the generic natural frequency.

steps.title: Design for a 10 kHz natural frequency
steps.instructions:
Keep LLP at 10 mH. Rearrange the f₀ equation to find CLP for a 10 kHz target. Enter your value, rerun the sweep and check f₀ using the phase crossing and the sample table. Leave the other three circuits as references.

If you also want the same damping, recompute RLP from Q = √(L/C)/R. Try tuning only C first, then both C and R. What moves along the frequency axis, and what changes shape?

steps.title: Record your design reasoning
steps.instructions: Record your hand-asymptote table, measured slopes and phase, before/after R and C, and the difference between f₀ and the −3 dB point. Explain why the notch has flat tails and a sharp dip, then predict how loss, source impedance or a real load would change one result.

lessons.title: Miller compensation and the nulling resistor
lessons.summary: Derive the Miller effect, see why the capacitor stabilizes the loop, and calculate how a series resistor moves the zero.

steps.title: Derive the effective input capacitance
steps.instructions: Open workspace and find the compensation capacitors between the high-impedance first-stage node and OUT. Start with ic = Cc·d(v₁−vout)/dt. At low frequency vout ≈ Av·v₁, so the current drawn from v₁ is Cc(1−Av)·dv₁/dt. If Av ≈ −100 and Cc = 2 pF, what is the input-side equivalent due to the branch?
steps.explanation: 1−(−100) = 101, so the 2 pF branch acts like about 202 pF at the first node at low frequency. Its current responds to the voltage difference across both terminals.

steps.title: Compare unity gain and phase
steps.instructions: Choose Open loop comparison. Use 20 pF load and 2 pF compensation. Read the first falling 0 dB crossing and then the phase of that same curve. Phase margin is 180° + ∠T. Which change comes from the capacitor by itself in this model?
options: It lowers the unity-gain frequency and increases the phase margin
It raises the unity-gain frequency and removes every pole
It leaves the loop response unchanged
steps.explanation: The uncompensated model crosses near 30.8 MHz with 3.1° margin. The capacitor moves crossover near 7.93 MHz and yields 37.4°. The dominant pole moves down, while the interaction of the two nodes moves the other pole up in this example.

steps.title: Calculate the capacitor-only zero
steps.instructions: The output-stage current contains gm₂·v₁ and a feedforward capacitor current. In the loop numerator they combine as gm₂−sCc. Set this to zero and convert the magnitude from rad/s to Hz. With gm₂ = 1 mS and Cc = 2 pF, where is the zero?
options: 79.6 MHz in the left half plane
79.6 MHz in the right half plane
1 kHz in the right half plane
steps.explanation: s = gm₂/Cc is positive, so the zero is in the right half plane. Its frequency magnitude is gm₂/(2πCc). The factor 1−s/ωz raises the magnitude slope and adds phase lag.

steps.title: Find the series resistor that nulls the zero
steps.instructions: Put Rz in series with Cc in the feedback branch. Its admittance is Yc = sCc/(1+sRzCc). Replace sCc with Yc in gm₂−Yc and clear the fraction. The numerator becomes gm₂[1+sCc(Rz−1/gm₂)]. What resistor makes the coefficient of s zero for gm₂ = 1 mS?
steps.explanation: Rz = 1/gm₂ = 1 kΩ. The model has no finite compensation zero. The poles still shape crossover and phase margin. At the default load, nulling alone gives about 42.8° against a 60° goal.

steps.title: Move the zero through infinity
steps.instructions: Keep the 20 pF load and 2 pF capacitor. Enter 500 Ω, 1 kΩ, and 2 kΩ in the series resistor control. Predict each zero using s_z = 1/[Cc(1/gm₂−Rz)], then check the table. What happens at 2 kΩ?
options: The zero returns to the right half plane at 79.6 MHz
The zero stays at infinity for all larger resistors
The zero moves to the left half plane at a magnitude of 79.6 MHz
steps.explanation: 1/gm₂−Rz is negative, so s_z is negative. The left-half-plane factor gives phase lead. The series resistor also changes the poles, so read the whole loop curve rather than adding a fixed margin.

steps.title: Explain the design tradeoff
steps.instructions: Record first unity frequency and phase margin for the capacitor alone, 1 kΩ, and 2 kΩ. Predict what a larger capacitor does to bandwidth, then test it. Explain the 202 pF approximation, why the resistor belongs in series, and why the final choice must be checked across load and gm₂ variation.

lessons.title: Ahuja compensation for op amps
lessons.summary: Compare direct Miller and current-buffered compensation, then see how load and buffer bandwidth change the loop.

steps.title: Trace direct Miller feedforward
steps.instructions: Open workspace and find CC1/CC2 on the two-stage Miller reference. A first-stage voltage change reaches the output through the inverting second stage and directly through the capacitor. Which sign is the direct capacitor path relative to the inverting stage?
options: The capacitor carries no AC current
steps.explanation: The direct path bypasses the stage inversion. In the simple model it produces a right-half-plane zero near gm₂/(2πCc) in Hz, which adds phase lag while raising the magnitude slope.

steps.title: Return compensation current through a buffer
steps.instructions: Open loop comparison. In the ideal Ahuja model the capacitor sees a low-impedance AC input at the buffer. Where does the current go?
options: Back to the high-impedance first-stage node
Directly forward from the first-stage node to the output
Only into the supply at every frequency
steps.explanation: The common-gate-style current buffer copies the output-derived compensation current back into the first stage. The ideal model removes the direct feedforward zero.

steps.title: Compare at the same capacitive load
steps.instructions: In Open loop comparison set Output load to 20 pF and Buffer pole to 50 MHz. Read the first 0 dB crossing and phase margin table. Which idealized comparison meets the 60° target?
options: The ideal Ahuja response does; direct Miller is below target
Direct Miller does; ideal Ahuja is below target
Both have the same phase margin
steps.explanation: At 20 pF the model gives about 37° for direct Miller and 81° for ideal Ahuja. Track each crossing separately because the curves cross 0 dB at different frequencies.

steps.title: Test the buffer assumption
steps.instructions: Keep the output load at 20 pF. Move Buffer pole from 50 MHz to 10 MHz and read the finite-buffer row again. What conclusion fits this experiment?
options: The finite buffer can miss the margin target even when the ideal model passes
The buffer pole cannot affect the loop
Ahuja compensation guarantees stability at every load
steps.explanation: The copied feedback current now has appreciable phase shift near crossover. This classroom model gives roughly 16° for the slow buffer, so the ideal-buffer prediction is inadequate.

steps.title: Record your design reasoning
steps.instructions: Record loop crossings and phase margins at two loads and at both 10 MHz and 50 MHz buffer settings. Explain what happens to the direct Miller zero, why a finite buffer matters, and how you would verify a transistor implementation for headroom, PVT, maximum load, transient settling and supply rejection.

lessons.title: Build a current reference and bias a mirror
lessons.summary: Set a 5 µA operating point, size from measured current density, and verify the mirror at a specified load.

steps.title: Translate the spec to a bias point
steps.instructions: The signal transistor needs 100 µS transconductance. Choose gm/ID = 20 V⁻¹ as a starting point. What drain current do you budget?
steps.explanation: ID = gm/(gm/ID) = 100 µS ÷ 20 V⁻¹ = 5 µA. Check the actual operating point after choosing width, length and terminal voltages.

steps.title: Size from current density
steps.instructions: A pilot sweep gives ID/W ≈ 0.5 µA/µm at the selected L, VDS, VSB, temperature and gm/ID. What total width aims at 5 µA?
steps.explanation: W = ID/(ID/W) ≈ 10 µm. A density from a different length, terminal bias, process or temperature can lead to a different width estimate.

steps.title: Set the reference and verify the mirror
steps.instructions:
Open workspace for simple_bias_fixture. RSET goes from 1.8 V to the diode-connected NMOS in the reference branch. The output device shares its gate. VCLAMP holds the output at 1.4 V so you can test the sink under a known load.

Run the testbench at the starter RSET and inspect V(vset) and the two source currents. Estimate RSET ≈ (1.8 − VSET)/5 µA, then trim it. A larger RSET usually lowers current. Re-run after each edit. In Results inspect the lower output MOS bias point. Check that the mirror sinks 4.5–5.5 µA and has at least 50 mV of model saturation margin. Record |ID|/W in µA/µm and gm/ID in V⁻¹. If you change width, match the reference and output geometry and repeat the operating-point check.

steps.instructions: Record the selected W, L and RSET. Give the measured reference and output currents, gm/ID, current density, and saturation margin. Explain why matched geometry can stabilize a ratio even when the absolute reference current drifts.

steps.title: Trace the stacked bias voltages
steps.instructions: Open workspace to inspect the cascode cell. A diode-connected reference stack establishes both gate biases. Why add the upper common-gate transistor?
options: It holds the lower output device’s drain steadier as OUT changes
It removes the need for output voltage headroom
It generates a fixed, process-independent current
steps.explanation: Holding the lower device’s drain steadier reduces channel-length modulation in that branch and increases output resistance. The upper device also needs its own drain-source headroom and can see body effect.

steps.title: Measure output resistance and the compliance knee
steps.instructions:
Open workspace for cascode_bias_fixture. Adjust its RSET for roughly 5 µA at the 1.4 V clamp. Measure the voltage at the top of the diode stack to estimate RSET. Run testbenches to sweep both outputs and collect operating points. The simple mirror shares the reference exercise’s settings. Keep both near 5 µA at the nominal clamp for a fair comparison.

In Results inspect |I(VCLAMP)| for each saved sweep. Estimate rout = ΔV/ΔI from 1.20 V and 1.50 V. The 5% flatness knee is the lowest sampled point after which the curve stays within 5% of its 1.4 V current. lessons.title: Widlar bandgap reference
lessons.summary: Weight a PTAT voltage to cancel the falling base–emitter voltage. Trim an editable GF180 circuit, then compare measured startup before and after layout.

steps.title: Find the two temperature slopes
steps.instructions: Work with identical emitter areas and a 10:1 current ratio. At a fixed density ratio, which quantities have opposite temperature slopes?
steps.explanation: VBE is the CTAT term in the operating region. ΔVBE = (kT/q)ln(J1/J2) grows with the absolute temperature.

steps.title: Calculate the first-order trim
steps.instructions: Find the PTAT slope using k/q ≈ 86.17 µV/K. Which R2/R3 offsets a −1.8 mV/°C junction slope with J1/J2=10?
steps.explanation: Divide 1.8 mV/°C by 0.1984 mV/°C to get about 9.07. The room-temperature ΔVBE itself is about 59.56 mV.

steps.title: Check slope and curvature
steps.instructions: Open temperature study. Use a 10:1 current ratio and R2/R3 = 9.07. Look at the drift graph from −40 to 125 °C. What remains?

steps.title: Predict both resistor settings

steps.title: Convert both voltages to currents
steps.instructions: With equal sense voltages and matched mirrors, which currents are summed into the output mirror?
options: Vf and ΔVf as unscaled series voltages
steps.explanation: The loop creates CTAT Vf/R2 and PTAT ΔVf/R3. The output resistor converts their sum to voltage.

steps.title: Choose a sub-1 V output
steps.instructions: The summed current is 12.38 µA. What output voltage results from R4=50 kΩ?

lessons.title: Differential pairs and common-mode range
lessons.summary: Separate current steering from common-mode headroom in a SKY130 differential pair.

steps.title: Predict the current steering
steps.instructions: With a small positive INP−INN, which drain moves down first?
options: The drain on the INP branch
The drain on the INN branch
Both move down by the same amount
steps.explanation: Higher gate voltage initially steers more tail current into the INP device. More drop across its load resistor pulls its drain down.

steps.title: Run the experiment and read the evidence
steps.instructions: Run the two sweeps. In the differential sweep VDIFF moves INP while INN is held at 0.90 V, so common mode also moves by half the input excursion. Read left-current share at both ends and at zero. In the common-mode sweep, VDIFF and VOFF keep INP−INN at 10 mV. Use the marked usable interval. At its low end compare V(TAIL) against the tail device’s required VDS.

steps.title: Explain it at the whiteboard
steps.instructions:
The amplifier loses gain as both inputs move down together while their difference remains 10 mV. What node and device would you check first?

Use a schematic sketch or name the controlling nodes. State one prediction, two measured values, and one tradeoff. Follow-up: Explain why increasing the tail current can change both gain and usable common-mode range.

lessons.title: Choosing PMOS or NMOS input pairs
lessons.summary: Compare complementary input stages by tracing real common-mode and drain headroom, then choose a polarity for a source.

steps.title: Read the headroom stack
steps.instructions: For a low common-mode signal in these conventional single-tail topologies, which pair is the better starting candidate?
options: PMOS input pair with a top tail source
NMOS input pair with a bottom tail source
Either pair has the same range regardless of bias
steps.explanation: The PMOS input sources sit above their gates. A bottom NMOS tail must fit below the input devices. Loads and supply determine the final usable range.

steps.title: Run the experiment and read the evidence
steps.instructions: Run both common-mode sweeps. Each has a 10 mV input difference and a 1.8 V supply. The usable range keeps total current within 20% and differential gain above 70% of their values at 0.70 V. Compare both measured currents at 0.70 V before comparing gain or noise. Start with the saved pair sizes and bias, then trim VBIAS to keep the two tail currents within 20% of each other. Make a polarity choice for a sensor whose common mode sits near ground and one that sits near VDD. Check the measured range against each actual sensor requirement.

lessons.title: Gain, output swing, and transistor headroom
lessons.summary: Use three SKY130 drain sweeps to measure why gain collapses when the output transistor runs out of headroom.

steps.title: Predict which slope changes
steps.instructions: As a common-source drain is pushed toward its source, which slope usually makes its gain collapse?
options: The drain current stops responding to drain voltage
Gate current becomes the intended signal path
steps.explanation: The channel enters its resistive region. A large change in drain current for a small change in drain voltage means lower output resistance and less voltage gain.

steps.title: Run the experiment and read the evidence
steps.instructions: Keep VG at 0.64, 0.65 and 0.66 V in the three benches. Run the drain sweeps and plot I(VD). ngspice uses the voltage-source convention, so the drain current magnitude is −I(VD). Compare the computed gm, ro and gain at VDS = 0.08 V and 0.80 V. Use the 50 kΩ load estimate to explain why intrinsic gain alone overstates actual stage gain.

steps.title: Explain it at the whiteboard
steps.instructions:
You need more gain at the same supply. How would you decide between a longer channel, more current, and a cascode?

lessons.title: Slew rate and precision settling
lessons.summary: Use one SKY130 follower to separate linear settling, current-limited motion, and DC tracking error.

steps.title: Find the additional bottleneck
steps.instructions: Phase margin is good on the small-signal test. What can still dominate settling for a large input step?
options: Limited charging current and the output load
DC gain alone determines every transient
steps.explanation: The loop can be locally stable and still saturate during a large transition. The capacitor can only move as quickly as the available source or sink current allows.

steps.title: Run the experiment and read the evidence
steps.instructions: Compare a 20 mV step on 2 pF with a 500 mV step on 2 pF, then put the same 500 mV step on 8 pF. Compare the falling steps at both loads as well. The edge begins at 2 µs. Look at the 10–90% slope, where the output first looks linear in time, and how long it takes to enter and stay within 2% of its final excursion. Compare the final DC error to a 2% band referenced to the command as well.

steps.title: Explain it at the whiteboard
steps.instructions:
An op amp with good phase margin misses an ADC’s large-step settlement deadline. How would you use two step amplitudes and two load values to isolate the cause?

lessons.title: Transistor and resistor noise budgets
lessons.summary: Measure how source resistance and device noise combine in a real amplifier over a declared bandwidth.

steps.title: Add noise correctly
steps.instructions: Two independent noise sources each contribute 10 µV RMS after referral to the same node and band. What is the total?
steps.explanation: Independent variances add. sqrt(10² + 10²) gives about 14.1 µV. A parent total and its own component traces overlap and must be counted once.

steps.title: Run the experiment and read the evidence
steps.instructions: Run the 1 kΩ and 100 kΩ source fixtures from 10 Hz to 1 MHz. Compare integrated input-referred and output noise, the low-frequency slope, and contributor names in Results. Change the source resistance as a follow-up and check where the dominant mechanism changes. Identify how a wider input device might affect flicker noise, source loading, and bandwidth together.

steps.title: Explain it at the whiteboard
steps.instructions:
Your source resistance went up by 100×. Explain why resistor noise voltage density goes up by 10× and why total system RMS need not do the same.

Use a schematic sketch or name the controlling nodes. State one prediction, two measured values, and one tradeoff. Follow-up: How would you handle a detector capacitance that changes the transfer function as you resize the input pair?

lessons.title: Offset, device area, and mismatch yield
lessons.summary: Separate a systematic load error from sampled threshold mismatch before choosing a yield improvement.

steps.title: Choose the correction
steps.instructions: Larger devices halve the offset spread but the mean is roughly unchanged. What would you inspect first to shift the mean?
options: Systematic load imbalance or bias asymmetry
Increase area again and expect the mean to converge to zero
steps.explanation: A deterministic load difference affects the center of the distribution. Device area mainly reduces the modeled random variance.

steps.title: Run the experiment and read the evidence
steps.instructions: Run 64 seeded trials per area. Compare the two histograms, sample mean, standard deviation and samples passing ±8 mV input-referred offset. RL starts at 15.3 kΩ and RR at 15 kΩ. Match RL to RR in both cells as a follow-up and repeat the same seed. The teaching solver varies the stated threshold parameter, keeping the nominal schematic and mismatch distribution separate.

steps.title: Explain it at the whiteboard
steps.instructions:
The typical design meets spec but samples fail near one side of a symmetric offset limit. What measurements separate mean shift, random spread, and global process movement?

Use a schematic sketch or name the controlling nodes. State one prediction, two measured values, and one tradeoff. Follow-up: Explain what 64 seeded teaching trials can and cannot tell you about a production failure rate.

lessons.title: Dynamic comparator delay and kickback
lessons.summary: Trace reset, current steering, and regeneration in a transistor-level clocked comparator.

steps.title: Predict the slower decision
steps.instructions: Which input produces the longer decision delay in this latch?
options: Overdrive cannot affect a clocked latch
steps.explanation: The weaker initial imbalance takes longer to grow to a logic-level difference. The common mode and clock slope can affect both cases.

steps.title: Run the experiment and read the evidence
steps.instructions: Compare 3 mV and 40 mV input overdrive at 0.90 V common mode. Read the time from the clock edge at 20 ns to OUTN−OUTP reaching 0.9 V. Then select INP or INN and inspect its disturbance relative to the corresponding ideal source. Try changing RP and RN together as a follow-up and explain the difference between source disturbance and decision delay.

steps.title: Explain it at the whiteboard
steps.instructions:
The latch works with an ideal source but corrupts an ADC with a high-impedance source. Where does the disturbance come from and how would you test a fix?

Use a schematic sketch or name the controlling nodes. State one prediction, two measured values, and one tradeoff. Follow-up: Explain how a preamplifier or isolation switch trades off power, latency and kickback.

lessons.title: Sampling, capacitor DACs, and SAR code errors
lessons.summary: Measure acquisition error and a real switch pedestal, then repair an incorrect SAR MSB capacitor.

steps.title: Choose the noise tradeoff
steps.instructions: If the sampling capacitor is four times larger, what happens to ideal sampled RMS thermal noise?
steps.explanation: Thermal variance is kT/C, so the RMS voltage is proportional to 1/√C. More capacitance also takes more charge and can slow acquisition.

steps.title: Capture the acquisition and MSB faults
steps.instructions: The switches track the input until 50 ns, then hold it. At 75 ns the MSB bottom plate steps by 1.6 V. Compare the fast and slow drivers, the hold pedestal, the estimated kT/C noise and the measured MSB step. A high-resolution noise-budget example allows 60 µV RMS at 300 K, which requires about 1.15 pF. This four-bit capacitor fixture is used to show how a bit-weight error moves a decision threshold. Keep C3 at 650 fF for this run.

steps.title: Repair the capacitor weight
steps.instructions: Choose Open circuit and set C3 to 800 fF while leaving the other capacitors and fixtures fixed. Rerun. Check that the MSB step is within 25 mV of 0.80 V and compare the estimated code at 0.76 V before and after the repair. The fast driver should acquire within 15 mV.

steps.title: Explain it at the whiteboard
steps.instructions:
A SAR produces an early transition into the upper half of its codes. How do you separate an MSB-weight error from a slow input driver or switch pedestal?

Use a schematic sketch or name the controlling nodes. State one prediction, two measured values, and one tradeoff. Follow-up: Explain why a larger sampling capacitor can solve a noise problem while creating a settling problem.

lessons.title: LDO dropout, load transients, and stability
lessons.summary: Use a SKY130 PMOS pass transistor and error amplifier to distinguish headroom limits from a ringing loop.

steps.title: Identify dropout
steps.instructions: The gate drive has reached its useful limit and VOUT falls as VIN drops. Which test does that indicate?
steps.explanation: The pass device needs drain-source voltage to deliver the load current. Once the loop has used up its drive, the output can no longer follow the target.

steps.title: Run the experiment and read the evidence
steps.instructions: Run the dropout, load-step, ESR, supply-step and power-on fixtures. Compare the two 25-to-100 µA load steps at 120 pF. Only the ESR changes. Find when the output stops ringing and remains within 2% of 1.20 V. Compare the lower supply limit with startup and line-step results. The external reference and amplifier bias are supplied by the fixture, so the ramp isolates regulator behavior.

steps.title: Explain it at the whiteboard
steps.instructions:
A load step rings at high supply, and the same circuit has low output near minimum supply. How would you tell which failure is a stability problem and which is dropout?

Use a schematic sketch or name the controlling nodes. State one prediction, two measured values, and one tradeoff. Follow-up: How would you repeat the check over load, capacitor tolerance, ESR and process before approving a capacitor substitution?

lessons.title: Debug a post-layout settling failure
lessons.summary: Find a layout parasitic that pushes a passing schematic past its settling deadline, then repair and rerun.

steps.title: Localize the failure
steps.instructions: The same stimulus passes on the schematic and fails after extraction. What should you compare first?
options: The same before/after node and the parasitics on its path
An unrelated supply pin on a different fixture
Two simulations with different load and stimulus
steps.explanation: Hold stimulus and load fixed, find the first node where traces diverge, and inspect the added R and C on that signal path.

steps.title: Reproduce the extracted timing miss
steps.instructions: Open Layout and keep the vout route at 0.20 µm. Run extracted interconnect. Save evidence that the schematic settles by 50 ps and the extracted trace misses.

steps.title: Change the route and prove the fix
steps.instructions: In Layout select the vout path and change its width. Try 0.40 µm, then compare it to 0.80 µm. Rerun the same experiment. Save a geometrically connected width that settles within 50 ps after extraction.

steps.title: Explain it at the whiteboard
steps.instructions:
The 0.20 µm route fails. Why might widening the route to 0.40 µm pass while widening it again to 0.80 µm misses the target?

lessons.title: Build an SPI register peripheral
lessons.summary: Read and write four registers in Mode 0. Discard short, long and invalid-address writes, and release MISO when deselected.

steps.title: Decide when a write can commit
steps.instructions: Which event can commit a valid write in this 16-bit SPI protocol?
options: Chip select rises after exactly 16 bits with a valid write address
The eighth bit arrives, even if the frame ends early
Any rising edge of SPI clock
steps.explanation: Treat each frame as a transaction. Commit only at frame end after exactly one command byte and one data byte.

steps.title: Inspect the frame and interface
steps.instructions: Open the RTL and find the command decoder, bit count, frame-end condition and return-bit update.

steps.title: Repair write commit and run the reference bench
steps.instructions: Read and write four registers in Mode 0. Discard short, long and invalid-address writes, and release MISO when deselected.

steps.title: Explain the framing rule
steps.instructions: Explain why committing on chip-select rise with an exact count prevents corruption. Describe when MISO may change in Mode 0.
